statement: On a 6 by 6 board of squares, a strip is a line of four squares side by side, going either across or down. How many different strips are there on the board?

choices.misconception: I divided the 36 squares by 4, as if the strips could not overlap.
I fitted strips without overlapping: one in each row and one in each column.
I counted the strips going across but forgot the ones going down.
I thought each row holds 6 - 4 = 2 strips, forgetting to add 1 for the first starting position.

hints: Where can the leftmost square of a strip going across be?
Slide a strip along one row and count its starting positions. Every row behaves the same way, and strips going down are the same count turned on its side.
A strip going across can start in column 1, 2 or 3, so each row holds 3 strips.

solutions.reliable: In one row, a strip of 4 squares can start in column 1, 2 or 3: 3 positions. With 6 rows that is 18 strips going across, and in the same way 18 strips going down, so 36 altogether. The transferable idea: a window of length k slides into n - k + 1 positions along a line of length n.

whyOnTest: Sliding-window counting: overlapping positions all count, and the starting-position count n - k + 1 is where off-by-one errors live.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
